ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Wilma Rudolph

code.originalText: Review three weeks after awake craniotomy: pathology and molecular diagnosis, steroid taper, steroid-related hyperglycemia, falls, and the plan for radiotherapy with temozolomide

text.paragraph: Review three weeks after awake craniotomy, before radiotherapy with temozolomide. [S]

Ms. Rudolph returns three weeks after an awake left frontal craniotomy. The surgeons removed all of the enhancing tumor, stopping at the mapped language sites, and the MRI the next day showed no residual enhancing tumor. Her speech was slower for three days after surgery and then came back to normal; she went home on the third day, having had heparin injections in hospital to prevent clots. She has had no seizure. The right hand is nearly back to normal, though fine buttons are still slow. The physical therapist saw her a week ago and gave her a home exercise program and a cane for uneven ground. She is now on dexamethasone 2 mg twice a day. Her fingerstick glucose readings at home have been 140 to 180 mg/dL after meals, and she is thirsty in the evenings. The pathology is glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with MGMT promoter methylation, and the tumor board has reviewed it with Dr. Brzezinski. She has met the radiation oncologist and had her planning scan, and starts radiotherapy with temozolomide on Monday. She has had no thoughts of self-harm. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-07-29; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well; weight 69.4 kg; blood pressure 132/80, pulse 76
Left frontal incision healed, staples out; no swelling or fluid collection
Fluent, no word-finding pauses; naming and repetition intact
No pronator drift; right grip 5-/5, finger tapping slightly slow; hip flexors 5/5 on both sides; rises from a chair without using her arms
No leg swelling; calves soft; left calf slightly smaller than the right

Three weeks of headaches on waking, with ten days of pauses in finding words and clumsiness of the right hand, in a previously well woman of 54: an intracranial lesion must be excluded. MRI of the brain with and without contrast booked for tomorrow morning, and neuro-oncology review booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem; no symptom of her real illness was made public. Superseded when the MRI showed a brain mass.

Left posterior frontal ring-enhancing mass, 3.8 cm, with central necrosis, surrounding edema and 5 mm midline shift, next to the language and motor areas; presumed high-grade glioma, with no primary cancer elsewhere on CT; tissue diagnosis pending
S — Synthetic imaging diagnosis before surgery; superseded by the pathology.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, left posterior frontal lobe, MGMT promoter methylated, after gross total resection of the enhancing tumor; synthetic modern detail linked to her publicly reported brain cancer
S — Synthetic histology, molecular result and location; brain cancer is documented as the cause of her death (D), and nothing more about it was made public.

Late effects of childhood poliomyelitis: paralysis of the left leg in early childhood, treated with a metal brace, a special shoe, massage and heat, with full recovery of walking by about age 12 and a later career as an Olympic sprinter; no new weakness, fatigue or pain now to suggest post-polio syndrome
S — Documented childhood polio (D); the current absence of new symptoms is synthetic.
Vasogenic cerebral edema around the left frontal mass, with 5 mm midline shift, causing headache and contributing to the language and right-hand symptoms; treated with dexamethasone
S — Synthetic finding on the first MRI.
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia on dexamethasone: random glucose 168 mg/dL, with an A1c of 5.6% before steroids
S — Synthetic common effect of dexamethasone; resolved after the taper.

list.item:
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, left frontal, MGMT promoter methylated, after gross total resection (C71.1). The integrated WHO CNS5 diagnosis is glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype: no IDH mutation on immunostaining or sequencing, with necrosis, microvascular proliferation, a TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification and chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss. MGMT promoter methylation and complete resection of the enhancing tumor in a fit woman of 54 are the most favorable factors this tumor has, and methylation predicts benefit from temozolomide. The tumor board recommends radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2 (140 mg for 1.84 m2), then six cycles of adjuvant temozolomide; tumor-treating fields will be discussed for the adjuvant phase. She was screened for open trials; none she was eligible for is open now. Baseline blood count, kidney and liver tests allow treatment. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests drawn today. [S]
Radiotherapy with temozolomide 140 mg at bedtime every day from Monday for six weeks.
Ondansetron 30 to 60 minutes before each dose.
Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim three times a week from the first day of temozolomide.
Blood count weekly at the radiation clinic.
Do not drive.

Vasogenic cerebral edema, better after resection (G93.6). Edema and midline shift less on the postoperative MRI; no headache. The taper can continue. [S]
Dexamethasone 2 mg daily for one week, then 1 mg daily for one week, then stop.
Report headache, nausea or new weakness during the taper.

Steroid-induced hyperglycemia (R73.9). Random glucose 168 mg/dL with home readings up to 180 after meals on dexamethasone, from an A1c of 5.6% before steroids: steroid-induced hyperglycemia, expected to resolve with the taper. No drug treatment is needed at these levels. [S]
Fingerstick glucose before supper daily until off dexamethasone.
Call for readings above 250 mg/dL.
Fewer sweet drinks and refined carbohydrates while on the steroid.

Late effects of childhood poliomyelitis (B91). Legs strong on both sides and gait steady. The physical therapist found mild right-sided weakness after surgery on top of a left calf that was weakened by polio in childhood; her risk of falling is higher during treatment because of fatigue, steroid effects on muscle, and any change in the tumor. [S]
Home exercise program and a cane for uneven ground.
Leg strength at each visit.

Left frontal mass, presumed high-grade glioma (D49.6). Superseded by the pathology. [S]
Problem resolved.

Follow-up: Radiotherapy with temozolomide from Monday for six weeks, with weekly blood counts at the radiation clinic. Primary care review at the end of radiotherapy. Call for fever, bruising, a seizure, new weakness or headache. Next scheduled visit 2026-09-14: end of six weeks of radiotherapy with daily temozolomide: blood counts, liver tests, Pneumocystis prophylaxis, fatigue, mood, tumor-treating fields and an early palliative care referral. [S]
